--- ## title: "Converted Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: default css: ../../custom2.css pagetitle: 'Survival estimation' slide-number: true echo: false lang: en --- # Introduction {visibility="hidden"} ## {content-align="center" style="font-size: 160%;"}
**Estimating survival using telemetry** ![](figs/radiotelemetry.jpg){height="10cm"} ![](figs/bbee.png){height="10cm"} ::: {style='font-size: 60%;'} Applied Population Dynamics WILD 5700/7700 :::
## Introduction Options for estimating survival: - Telemetry * Binomial model * Kaplan-Meier model ::: {.fragment} - Age distribution data * Often used but rarely valid ::: ::: {.fragment} - Capture-mark-recapture * Covered in the previous lecture ::: # Telemetry ## Telemetry ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='60%'} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Pros * Fate is often known * Analysis can be straight-forward * Much additional information can be obtained ::: {.fragment} Cons * Batteries don't last as long as bands * When fate is unknown, analysis can be hard * Transmitters may influence vital rates and behavior ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='40%'} ![](figs/saltie.png){width="100%"} ![](figs/Banded_penguin.jpg){width="100%"} ::: ::: ## Binomial model ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}
Design * $n$ animals are randomly sampled and monitored over a fixed time interval. ::: {.fragment} * The fates of all animals are known at end of the study period. ::: ::: {.fragment} * $x$ of the $n$ animals survive. ::: ::: {.fragment} * The estimate of survival over the time interval is given by: $$ \hat{S} = \frac{x}{n} $$ ::: ::: ## Binomial model ::: {style='font-size: 100%;'} Assumptions 1. Fates are independent 2. Fates are known 3. All individuals are exposed to mortality during the same time interval ::: {.fragment} When [censoring]{.key-term} occurs, assumptions (2) and (3) are violated. ::: ::: {.fragment} Censoring occurs when the time of mortality is not directly observed. ::: ::: ## Censoring Right censoring - Occurs when animals leave the sample before they die. - Examples: * Battery failure * Emigration ::: {.fragment} Left censoring and interval censoring are rarely a concern. ::: ::: {.fragment} If censoring occurs, the Kaplan-Meier estimator is more appropriate than the binomial model. ::: ## Censoring
::: {.framed-img} ![](figs/censoring.png){height="11cm"} ::: ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Diamonds indicate mortality. Circles indicate censoring.
Black lines show the observation period. :::
## Kaplan-Meier
$$ \hat{S}_t = \prod_{j: t_i \le t}\left(\frac{r_j - d_j}{r_j}\right) $$ $S_t$ -- probability of surviving to time $t$
$r_j$ -- number of individuals *at risk* prior to time $t$
$d_j$ -- number of mortalities prior to time $t$ ## Kaplan-Meier in R ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-survival_files/figure-revealjs/kapmeier-1.png){width=960} ::: :::
[Deer capture video](https://youtu.be/Mgp46izlfeo)
## Kaplan-Meier ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}
**Critical Assumption**: Censoring must be independent of survival * It's fine if transmitters fail randomly * It's a problem if they fail because of mortality
::: {.fragment} *Consequence of violating this assumption*: If an animal dies, but you mistakenly right censor it because you think its battery died, survival will be over-estimated. ::: ::: # Age distributions ## Age distribution data Standard practice * We have a pile of wings that can be aged * We assume the age ratios tell us something about survival
![](figs/dove_wing.jpg){height="7cm"} ::: {.fragment} [**There are many problems with this approach.**]{.callout--caution} :::
## Alternative scenario Suppose a cohort of individuals is monitored over time, so that we can obtain information about survival. $$ n_{i+1,t+1} = n_{i,t}S_{i,t} $$ ::: {.fragment} $$ S_{i,t} = \frac{n_{i+1,t+1}}{n_{i,t}} $$ :::
::: {.fragment} All is well. This is a valid approach based on the binomial model. :::
## Age distributions The problem is that this... $$ S_{i,t} = \frac{n_{i+1,t+1}}{n_{i,t}} $$ ... is not the same as data from *standing age distribution*: $$ S_{i,t} = \frac{n_{i+1,t}}{n_{i,t}} $$
::: {.fragment} [**Several pitfalls are associated with this problem**.]{.callout--caution} :::
## Pitfall I
Standing age distribution data can't be used to estimate survival, unless... * Population is at the stable age distribution * $\lambda = 1$ ## Pitfall II
**Population reconstruction** refers to the calculation of the abundance and age distribution of a cohort at some initial time, usually based on *ages at death*.
::: {.fragment} This is only possible if we know the ages of death for **all** individuals in the cohort. :::
::: {.fragment} Shouldn't use this type of *reconstruction data* as real data in a subsequent analysis. ::: ## Pitfall III
The age data are biased * Age data not representative of actual age distribution. * Hunting, trapping, and capture-recapture methods do not evenly sample the population. ## Avoiding the pitfalls
When estimating survival, it is always good to... * Collect more than 1 year of data. * Follow multiple cohorts of individuals over long periods of time. * Estimate survival using telemetry or mark-recapture methods.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
